connection: The St Kilda wren is a subspecies of the Eurasian wren endemic to the St Kilda archipelago. It is known only from St Kilda, where it is larger, greyer and more heavily barred than mainland wrens.

The St Kilda field mouse is a subspecies of the wood mouse endemic to the St Kilda archipelago, where it lives on Hirta and Dùn. It is larger than mainland wood mice and is thought to have reached St Kilda on the boats of Viking settlers.
The Fair Isle wren is a subspecies of the Eurasian wren endemic to Fair Isle in Shetland. It is darker and larger than the mainland wren and feeds along the Fair Isle foreshore.

The Orkney vole is a subspecies of the common vole found on Orkney Mainland, Sanday, Westray, Rousay, South Ronaldsay, Burray, Eday, Shapinsay and Stronsay, and it is absent from the rest of the British Isles. It is larger than continental common voles and is thought to have been brought to Orkney by Neolithic people.

The Orkney charr is a cold-water fish that was endemic to Hoy in Orkney and is now listed as extinct. It has not been recorded on Hoy since the early twentieth century, although a very similar fish has been reported from the Isle of Skye.
The Arran whitebeam is a tree in the rose family found only on the island of Arran. It is an endemic whitebeam that arose through hybridisation involving rowan and rock whitebeam.

The Catacol whitebeam is a tree endemic to the Isle of Arran and is not found anywhere else in the world. It arose as a hybrid between rowan and the Arran cut-leaved whitebeam, and it is one of three endemic whitebeams on Arran.
The Shetland mouse-ear is an endemic variety of chickweed that now grows only on the island of Unst. It is a small cushion-forming plant of Unst and is not known from any other island today.

Sorex araneus grantii is a subspecies of the common shrew found only on the Scottish island of Islay. It differs from mainland shrews by its very grey flanks and its teeth, and it was once treated as a species of its own.
The red-billed chough in Scotland is concentrated on the islands of Islay and Colonsay. Those two islands are where Scotland's choughs breed.

The mice on Canna are believed to be a rare and distinct subspecies of wood mouse. A breeding stock of these Canna mice was removed before rats were cleared from the island, so the mouse would not be lost.

Colonsay and Oronsay hold a protected population of the European dark bee, Apis mellifera mellifera, and other honeybees are banned from the two islands so that it is not hybridised. The bees were gathered from elsewhere in Scotland and are now known as the Colonsay dark native bee.
The northern gannet takes its scientific name, Morus bassanus, from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth. The Bass Rock holds the world's largest colony of the northern gannet.
Ailsa Craig, in the Firth of Clyde, holds one of the world's largest colonies of the northern gannet. The northern gannet has nested on Ailsa Craig since the sixteenth century.

The Manx shearwater is a burrow-nesting seabird, and Rùm is one of three islands that hold most of the British and Irish breeding population. Manx shearwaters visit Rùm only at night and otherwise live at sea.
The white-tailed eagle was reintroduced to Rùm and then established a stronghold on Mull. Mull is one of the few places where this sea eagle can be seen.

source_title: List of moths of Great Britain (Zygaenidae)
connection: The slender Scotch burnet subspecies Zygaena loti scotica is listed from the islands of Mull and Ulva. It is a Red Data Book burnet moth of those two islands.

source_title: List of moths of Great Britain (Zygaenidae)
connection: Zygaena lonicerae jocelynae is a subspecies of the narrow-bordered five-spot burnet listed from the island of Skye. It is a Red Data Book burnet moth of Skye.
The Isle of May has its own unique race of house mice. That race of house mouse is known from the Isle of May and is treated as distinct from other house mice.
The Atlantic puffin has one of the largest colonies in the United Kingdom on the Isle of May. Puffins return to the Isle of May to breed on an island that has no foxes or rats.
The red-necked phalarope is a rare breeding bird in Britain, and Fetlar in Shetland is the most reliable place for it. This small wader breeds on Fetlar at the edge of its world range.

Red-necked wallabies were introduced to Inchconnachan, an island in Loch Lomond, in the 1940s and still live wild there. Inchconnachan is one of the few places outside Australia with a viable population of this wallaby.
The razorbill is an auk, and Handa holds the largest breeding colony of razorbills in the United Kingdom. No other British colony of the razorbill is larger than the one on Handa.
The common guillemot is an auk, and Handa holds the largest breeding colony of guillemots in the United Kingdom. No other British colony of the common guillemot is larger than the one on Handa.

The short-necked oil beetle is a flightless beetle whose young depend on solitary bees, and Coll is the most important site for it in the United Kingdom. The beetle was rediscovered on Coll after it had been missing from most of Britain for decades.
